items.script: My cousin lives far from our village, but we are learning each other's favourite expressions. Video calls were difficult because our internet was slow in the evening. Instead, we sent short voice notes and listened to them when the connection improved.

items.stem: Which instrument did the visiting musician actually play?
items.script: During the cultural evening, a visitor explained how different instruments make different sounds. She showed us a wooden flute and a modern violin, but the instrument she performed with for the audience was a traditional oud.

items.stem: Where did families meet the project coordinator?

items.stem: What did the pupil use to keep the phone working?
items.script: Our class exchanged messages with pupils from another island during a ferry trip. I remembered my headphones and a printed map, but the most useful item was a portable charger. It kept my phone working until I could send our arrival message.

items.stem: What did the families make together?
items.script: At the neighbourhood food workshop, families shared recipes from different places. We tasted sweet dates and a rice dish, but the activity everyone joined was making flatbread. We mixed the dough, rolled it into small circles and cooked it carefully on a hot plate.

listening2.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to Connections. Bilal, your class organised a language exchange with another school. How did the idea begin?
Bilal: A visitor spoke to us about regional words and expressions. We discovered that we knew different names for some everyday objects and wanted to learn more.
Interviewer: Did you travel to the other school?
Bilal: Not at first. We created short recordings and exchanged them online. Each recording included a word, its meaning and an example sentence.
Interviewer: How did you make the recordings clear?
Bilal: We spoke slowly and kept background noise low. Our teacher checked every recording before it was sent.
Interviewer: Was the exchange only about vocabulary?
Bilal: No. Pupils shared stories about family celebrations and school traditions. We learnt that people can have different customs but still enjoy many of the same activities.
Interviewer: What was difficult?
Bilal: Sometimes the same word meant different things. We asked for examples instead of guessing. This prevented misunderstandings.
Interviewer: When did the classes finally meet?
Bilal: At the end of term, we held a joint workshop in our school hall. Pupils worked in mixed groups and made illustrated phrase cards.
Interviewer: What will you do with the phrase cards?
Bilal: We plan to give them to younger pupils next semester. The project taught us to listen respectfully and ask better questions.
